parts.title: This Jar Was Once SAND! What Are Things Made Of? (Part 1) | The 7 Materials
parts.description:
One of these three snack boxes was once sand. Which one? Be a grain of sand and find out! Part 1 of Primary 3 Science, Diversity of materials: what are things made of?

In this part:
• Object or material? A spoon is an object; metal is its material
• Is a window a material? HOLD ON!
• Be a grain of sand: how sand becomes glass
• Look closer: sand melting in a furnace, shiny metal in a rock, oil into plastic, a clay bowl baked hard in a kiln
• Glass, metal, plastic and ceramic: where each one comes from
• Spot the hidden sparrow!

Key words: object, material, ceramic, clay.
Watch Part 2: your school shoe came from a tree?

Did you know? Plastic is usually long-lasting: it takes a long time to break down. So reuse it and recycle it.

TheOneApp, Explained: Singapore primary science, made fun. Play along with Pip, Basil and Momo: show fingers to lock in, keep score on your hand, beat the Buddies! Practise this topic in TheOneApp: School Lab 3.1 “What is it made of?”, Part (a) Count the parts. How many materials is a backpack made of? Press “Let's test it now!”.

Singapore Primary 3 Science (2023 syllabus): Diversity of materials: objects and materials, the 7 materials (Chapter 3, pp. 45–52). Also fits US NGSS 2-PS1-1 (Grade 2 to 3).
Try it at home: pick one object at home, like a school bag or a water bottle. Count its parts. What material is each part made of? Tell someone at home.
Singapore and the US: at the school canteen, the noodle bowl is ceramic, the spoon is metal and the window is glass. In the US (Grade 2 to 3), count the parts of a lunch box or a pair of sneakers: plastic, metal, fabric, rubber.

parts.title: Your School Shoe Came from a TREE? (Part 2) | The 7 Materials
parts.description:
Your school shoe came from a tree? Be a drop of white sap and find out! Part 2 of Primary 3 Science, Diversity of materials: the 7 materials.

In this part:
• Wood: from the trunks of trees (look closer at the planks)
• Be a drop of sap: how rubber can come from a rubber tree
• Look closer: white sap from a thin cut in the bark; the threads of a T-shirt, over and under
• Fabric: from animals or plants (cotton, wool, silk)
• Showdown: count the parts of a school shoe (one object, four materials)
• All seven materials, and a chant to remember them
• Spot the hidden sheep!

Key words: rubber, sap, fabric.
Watch Part 1 first! Next episode: snap it or bend it? We test the materials.

Did you know? Rubber trees once grew all over Singapore and Malaysia. And Charles Goodyear worked for more than five years to make rubber that stayed good in hot and cold weather.
